blocks.p: In the evening Rei could not stand still at home any more. The flat was too quiet. The cold by the door was too patient. So he put on his shoes and went out, without deciding where.

He walked down the hill to Ōji station in the last of the heat. The sun was low and orange behind the buildings, and the air still felt like the inside of a mouth. The cicadas in Asukayama park, the wooded hill beside the station, were so loud they drowned the traffic. Paper lanterns hung along the shopping street, and an old man was walking slowly ahead of him with a bundle of flowers and incense wrapped in a cloth, on his way to some family grave.

At the ticket gate Rei touched his Suica card to the reader. It gave its small bright beep, and the gate let him through. He took the first train that came, a Keihin-Tōhoku train with its sky-blue stripe, heading south into the city. It was crowded with people going home for the holiday, carrying suitcases and paper bags of gifts. A salaryman slept standing up, holding the strap, his tie loose. Two schoolgirls in summer uniforms shared one pair of earphones, a wire running from one ear to the other, and laughed at something on a phone. Rei got off at Nippori for no reason except that the doors opened, and he let the crowd carry him up and down the stairs until he was standing on the platform of the Yamanote line, the light-green loop line that circles central Tokyo.

blocks.cap: The Yamanote platform on the eve of Obon

blocks.p: The departure board flicked over, and over, and over, and Rei stayed where he was. A train came in. The station played its short bright jingle. The doors opened, took in a family dressed in matching yukata, and closed again. A yukata is a light cotton kimono that people wear in summer, to festivals and fireworks and on holiday evenings like this one. The train left without him.

At home, standing still had become unbearable. Here, at least, everything around him was going somewhere. He took out his phone and wrote the message he had been writing in his head since the voicemail.
where are you. just tell me you're somewhere.

He deleted the full stop, because Gin hated full stops in texts. Gin said they made everything sound like a man being fired from his job. Then Rei put it back, because he wanted Gin to feel the weight of it. Then he deleted it again and sent the message bare.

The three grey dots came up almost at once. The dots meant someone was typing on the other end. His whole body leaned toward them. It was the way he used to lean toward the front door when Gin was late. It was the old animal habit of a younger brother who has spent his life listening for one key in one lock.
The reply was kind. That was the first thing that was wrong, and he would not let himself see that it was wrong for another hour.
I'm okay, Rei. I promise I'm okay. You don't need to do all this.

They were the right words. It even used the right small name. The dots had come up fast. But the message itself arrived a beat late behind them. It was as if someone had watched him type, started to answer, and then paused to make sure the answer was correct.

Gin never paused to make sure. Gin answered wrong and fast, and then sent four more texts correcting himself. His thumbs had always been quicker than his judgement. And now Rei stood on a platform reading a version of him who had become, overnight, as patient and calm as a much older man.

There was a line in Gin's book about that. It was in a list of ways to spot a demon wearing a person, by someone sharing a room with it. Gin had rated this sign low, because it took time to see. The presentation is always slightly more consistent than a human would naturally be. A human has bad days, contradictions. A well-maintained cover has fewer of these. The smoothness itself is a tell. Real people are messier.

blocks.cap: The station crowds on the eve of Obon

blocks.p: The Obon crowds moved around him. There were paper fans, and children with plastic masks pushed up on their heads, and the smell of grilled corn drifting in from the food stalls outside the station. Families were carrying small lanterns home to set out for their dead. A woman beside him fanned herself with a folded train timetable, slowly, without looking up from her phone. He should have got on a train. He let three trains go.
He wrote back. all this what. tell me where you are and i'll stop.

He watched the dots. The dots thought about it. They appeared, and rested, and vanished, and appeared again. In the whole history of Rei's phone, Gin had never once made the dots think. The thing about to answer was choosing its words. And the one thing in the world it was being careful not to give him was a place.
So Rei decided to spend something he could never get back. He would set a test, with a small trap inside it.

He knew the memory exactly. It was the night of their mother's funeral. The funeral had run long, and he and Gin had slipped out to the konbini. Gin had bought him the wrong onigiri on purpose. An onigiri is a rice ball wrapped in seaweed, with something tucked in the middle. Gin chose the one Rei hated, with umeboshi inside, the sour red pickled plum. He did it because making Rei complain was the only way he knew to make him stop crying. Gin bought the wrong one three times before Rei laughed. Only the two of them in the whole world knew that it had taken three.
Rei wrote the memory almost right. He put salmon in it instead of plum. Then he asked. do you remember what you bought me after okaasan's. you remember how many times.
Okaasan is mother. He did not need to say the word funeral. Gin would know.

The dots came. The dots stayed a long while. Then the answer arrived, and it was so gentle it nearly broke him. It did not take the bait. It did not miss the bait either. It folded the bait into something warmer than the truth.
I remember I kept getting it wrong until you laughed. I'd get it wrong a hundred times if it worked, Rei. I'd do anything that worked.

It did not say salmon. It did not say umeboshi. It did not say three. It gave him only the shape of the memory, the love in it, the part that would be true whatever the details were. And it pointed that love straight at him, at the hands it wanted. It did it with a precision his real, clumsy, grieving brother had never once managed.
Rei sat down on the platform bench. A station attendant in white gloves glanced at him and decided he was only drunk.

This was the lesson Gin's casework had tried to teach him, and only now was his body learning it. The thing wearing Gin still had all of Gin's affection. What it had lost were the small facts, the ones that would pin it to one particular night. So it could never be caught out on facts, because it would always answer with feeling instead. And the feeling was real. It truly was Gin's. That was what made it the worst weapon ever turned on him. It was not a fake.

He had wanted it to fail the test. Instead it had passed by refusing to take it. Somewhere under his ribs, Rei felt his inner floor tip by the few degrees he had come to recognise. That was the price of being understood by something that was studying him.

He thought of another line from the same chapter. Gin had called it instrumental orientation, which only meant that a demon treats people as tools. Genuine relationships modulate based on the other party's needs. Demon engagement increases pressure when the practitioner is vulnerable and decreases when the practitioner is stable. Rei scrolled back up the thread. The warmest message had come in the minute after his hardest one. The thing had felt him sag onto the bench, through a screen, and leaned in.
He started a new message. He typed Gin, and a question mark, and then he stopped with his thumb over the send button.

There was a page in Gin's book about the hardest cases of all. These were the ones where a practitioner had known the person before a demon wore them. Gin had written it after two cases like that. The cadence is right and the content is wrong and the gap between them is a specific kind of grief that does not have a protocol. What I have found useful. Do not address the demon by the original person's name. The name is for the person. The classification is for what is in front of you. They are not the same thing.

Rei deleted the name. On the phone call, when he said it out loud, the name had reached someone. Gin had come up for four seconds. Here, typed into a thread the smooth voice was holding, the name would only be handed to the thing to use. He would keep it. He would save his brother's name for his brother.

Over the next hour, between the trains he still did not take, he noticed that the thing had a refrain. A refrain is a line that comes back again and again, like the chorus of a song. And when someone keeps coming back to the same line, that line is usually the wall holding up everything else.

Four times, each time dressed in a different kind of warmth, it told him to stop. You don't need to do all this. Let it go cold, Rei. Some cases close themselves. You'll make yourself ill. Each one sounded like real concern. But when he laid them side by side, every one of them was aimed at the same single thing. His looking. Not his safety. Not his sleep. His looking. It did not mind if he was frightened. It only minded if he was searching. The difference between those two things was a whole map of what it was protecting.

Gin had a rule for this, written for practitioners who knew the person before a demon wore them. Everything the demon tells you, everything it seems to offer, assume it is calculated. Ask why it wants you to have this information. The answer is usually more useful than the information itself. Rei turned the rule around. What did it want him not to have?

A place. A station exit, a district, a name on a doorbell. Any place would lead him back to Kita, to the veil over the ward, where the thing was doing its slow work of thinning. That was the wound in the world. It was widening the wound one reasonable favour at a time, so that the empty Thirteenth Seat would have a reason to be filled.

And it was in no hurry. That was the other thing the thread showed him, laid out end to end. It never pushed twice in a row. After every refusal it let a quiet minute go by, as if it had all the time there was. Gin had a paragraph about that too. Demons with operational history are more patient than any practitioner they will encounter. You have a career. They have centuries. Do not mistake demon patience for demon passivity. They are waiting because the right moment is not yet here. And under it was a line Rei had underlined without knowing why. What you can do is change what the patient demon is waiting for. If the moment requires you to be isolated, be not isolated.

He watched the refrain come round again, and he understood. He had not been talking to a liar. He had been talking to a gatekeeper, and the gate it kept was a place on a map. The warmth was sincere. The steering was the job. Both could be true from the same pair of thumbs, and they were. That was the new and terrible skill he was learning. He could read the love and the plan in the same sentence, as it arrived, without letting one cancel out the other.

At last he crossed to the next platform and boarded a Keihin-Tōhoku train heading north toward home, because he needed to be a body going somewhere. As the doors closed he sent the last text of the night. okay. i'll stop.
The dots came up fast. It was relief. Real relief. He could feel it through the glass of the screen. The thing that wore his brother was glad.
He sat with that. He had just lied to his brother for the first time in his life. And the part of Gin that was glad was exactly the part he most needed to disappoint.

The carriage swayed north through the dark. Outside, the city slid past in strips of light, apartment windows, a lit konbini, a level crossing with its bell ringing. Across the carriage a little girl held a lit Obon lantern in two careful hands. She was guiding home a dead person she had never met. Her grandmother sat beside her with a bag of peaches on her lap, nodding off. When the train reached Ōji, Rei did not get off. He rode three stops past his own, just to keep moving, and then crossed the platform and came back.

That night he lay down on top of the covers in his clothes, with the phone on the pillow beside his head. He thought about turning the sound off. He did not. Some animal part of him was still listening for one key in one lock.
Later, he would be very glad of that.
